Greet the dawn with eyes wide open

by Lilliae

Summary

There was only one person who could cook such a delicious meal. The very same only person who could enter and exit his home undetected when he refused to open it for anyone—because he had personally handed over the spare key.

Mydei.

The man who would spite him with terrible food when his jokes grew as stale as the bread he must have left uncovered just for him, or his methods in their latest spar was as slimy as the fish gutted but raw and unscaled. Who could now recall the whole truth but still prepared such a thing with care for the person responsible for his every death.

Amphoreus has become a real planet forged from the memories accumulated over millions of years.

Every citizen is bestowed all the memories that are rightfully their own, so there’s no escaping the actions Phainon took to prolong the cycles until a true hero could arrive with the new dawn.

But when Phainon is unable to see his own worth and face the tomorrow everyone had longed for, there are plenty of people at his side willing to help open his eyes to the truth.

Notes

chapters.title: Greet the dawn with eyes wide open
chapters.html:
The pale dawn had finally arrived and illuminated the path to a previously unimaginable tomorrow for Amphoreus.

So it was time for him to face the consequences of every transgression he committed in those 33,550,336 cycles as nothing but a false deliverer. One who couldn’t herald a new dawn: only drag on an endless dusk in the hope of delaying extinguishment of the sun that would plunge them into eternal night.

Someone unworthy of the title of hero and all its shining idealisms because his life burned itself away on the wick of hatred and Destruction.

And now everyone knew.

The very moment Irontomb’s control was shattered by the combined might of the Astral Express and the Chrysos Heirs, the gaze of Remembrance transformed Amphoreus from electrical signals and numbers into a planet as real as the rest of the universe beyond the true starry sky.

Something that could only be achieved by the accumulation of memories over 33,550,337 cycles. The Remembrance, that didn’t discriminate between the cycle that had ended it all and every cycle that came before it, merged them into one uninterrupted line of memory. Heedless of everything he had given to drag back the hands of time to the beginning over and over again, those memories became the basis of every living being in Amphoreus.

It should have been a celebration when his body was dragged from Irontomb and across the finish line he started towards: sprinted with determination to shatter fate, walked as lifetimes of failure wore away at him, and eventually crawled as his body crumbled to ash alongside his humanity. Another hero, the true deliverer, had succeeded and brought an end to his endless journey.

Instead, he was forced awake to stand before the other Chrysos Heirs as the recollection of all previous cycles became rightfully theirs once again. The horror, the fear—

He fled before he was forced to witness the rejection.

He knew. He already knew. Once he inherited the duty accompanied by memories and Coreflames, he knew beyond doubt that the people he once considered his friends… no, his family. Ones who could never replace all he had lost when Aedes Elysiae was destroyed by the black-robed swordsman—by himself. Who became the target of his own hatred—but flourished in their own place within his heart alongside the scorched remains of home. They would never accept him now.

Because they knew the truth. Every vile sin he committed because he could never fulfil their unified wish for the new dawn. Every stolen Coreflame. Every second of dread shadowed in a tattered black robe. Every new stain of gold on the corroded edge of his greatsword.

Just the impression of gold splattered on metal made his chest clench down into his stomach. The part of himself that could still flinch away from his own transgressions was the very first sacrifice his body carved out to make space for the Coreflames. But now, without an ambition to hold fast to, to justify those actions, himself, as a necessary evil to guarantee the future, he couldn’t stand the onslaught of memories.

The contempt. The scorn. The derision when they realised how far their precious Phainon, their deliverer, the carrier of their hopes and dreams, had fallen. A stranger. No longer human: everything resembling a person pared down to firewood for the sake of the Coreflames he had to carry to the distant end of a near impossible journey.

When they attempted to stop him through reason or force, he slaughtered them without remorse. Again and again.

His stomach twisted. He lurched and dry heaved into the bucket between his legs like he could regurgitate every terrible recollection—purge them from his body like poison and return to who he once was. Blissfully ignorant. A person who could hold a golden ideal in his heart and strive for it in earnest with a smile.

But so long as everyone else remembered it was pointless.

He dragged his hand across the back of his mouth. Nothing but spit and bile. His stomach realised it was futile and settled back down; the poison was in his veins, injected by none other than himself.

The bucket rattled as he kicked it to the side. He slumped back against the wall, head between his arms and knees as he tried to breathe through the acrid burn in his throat.

If only he could merge with the shadows of the wall and disappear somewhere he would never be seen again. To hide in this dingy corner of this bedroom forever.

It wasn’t reasonable but reason was no longer a familiar companion of his. He lost it sometime in the first fifty cycles when he realised Irontomb operated with logics he could never begin to grasp. Sometime after the four millionth cycle, when that first body broke down and no body afterwards could hope to last anywhere near as long, every Phainon who became Khaslana shed his own rationality and restraint for hatred and a mind that failed to process more than was needed to continue the cycles.

So he didn’t move. With the blackout curtain drawn shut, there was no knowing how much time had passed since he fled from his former friends and shut himself in his house. Enough time for his stomach to run out of food to retch.

Enough time for someone to knock on his front door. Once, and again some time later: consistent intervals that began short but gradually grew longer as he ignored them. Then they stopped and his heart clenched so tight his ears rang with relief that he was completely alone again. It was the state he was most familiar with in the way a tattered cloak still offered comfort.

He scrubbed at his face, hands tacky with blood everyone could now see for themselves, and closed his eyes to disappear into slumber.

Sleep was reminiscent of the assimilation process. The black tide gripped and pulled him to pieces, gouging into flesh turned back into electrical signals and prying him apart. Sloughing off limbs and thoughts turned into numbers among a sea of them. 

But it had been dark. He hovered on the restless edge between deep slumber and wakefulness. While the rest of him sank away, the one thing that remained untouched was the blazing hatred at his core. The one that annihilated itself with the need to burn bright enough to scorch the bars of fate to cinders.

The hours he slept were irrelevant. Nothing changed in the time between sleep and wakefulness. Alone in the dark.

Except he next stirred to a scent in the air. His stomach rumbled with realisation before his mind lifted from the haze of sleep. Fresh food. Inside the house.

Tipped onto his side where he curled into himself as he slept, he pushed himself from the floor. His stomach grumbled but he didn’t truly feel hungry—a consequence of the time spent dragging his half-cremated corpse around, made worse by his time in Irontomb—so there was no reason for him to sway on unsteady feet towards the bedroom door for food he didn’t even want. 

He opened the door. He lived alone. It was impossible for the aroma of food to waft through the rooms and creep under doorways while he was still wallowing on the floor.

Yet there was something new on the table. The entire house was shrouded in darkness but it was obvious when the silhouette of his low table was cleared of its usual books and antiques. He approached slowly, like prey anxious to avoid drawing attention to itself when a predator lurked nearby, but the unfamiliar objects didn’t vanish even when his shins bumped against the low table edge in front of the kline.

A tray with an assortment of dishware. A knife and spoon wrapped in a napkin. Another square cut of cloth underneath a small bowl of gently steaming water. A chalice of milk. Three covered dishes, but his hands clenched at his sides rather than open them. His stomach came louder, confused why he was hesitating to eat the meal so tantalisingly laid before him.

His hand trembled—fatigue, lack of food, fear of something he couldn’t name—but he closed it around the largest covering. When it lifted, the smell alone made his mouth water. A soup. The base seemed thin but it was full of vegetables, thin slices of meat, and herbs that gave rise to a pleasant aroma.

He moved onto the others. A platter of bread accompanied by soft cheese, and a plate of assorted berries and apples neatly sliced and arranged into a circle.

All of it was fresh and prepared with care. So much consideration that couldn’t have been for him yet deliberately placed in his house, as though the maker wanted to slap him across the face with it. If skulked back to the bedroom and pretended he never saw it, letting it go cold and then rotten on his table, then he would be discarding all that person’s efforts.

First he washed his hands in the small bowl of water and dried them on the cloth. Then he deliberated between his options. The cover on the stew would keep it warm a little longer and he needed the bread to clean the bowl, whereas the apple slices had been exposed to air and would swiftly brown.

The slice was cool against his fingertips and crisp between his teeth, flesh firm and sweet. Once he started he couldn’t stop.

The berries burst with sweetness. The stew was warm and filling. The bread was moist and the crust still flaky. The goats milk was cold from an icebox.

When he set the chalice down he wiped the napkin across his mouth and realised the rest of his face was wet too. He sniffled with a blocked nose as the tears fell too fast to catch with the rapid swipe of two shaky hands up his cheeks.

There was only one person who could cook such an exquisite meal. The very same only person who could enter and exit his home undetected—because he had personally handed over the spare key.

Mydei.

The same man who would spite him with terrible food when his jokes grew as stale as the bread he must have left uncovered just for him, or his methods in their latest spar was as slimy as the fish gutted but raw and unscaled. Who could now recall the whole truth but still prepared such a thing with care for the person responsible for his every death.

He needed to clean the dishware. He would. But the food was so comfortably warm in his stomach where it warmed him throughout. Despite only having woken, he was so drowsy he trudged to the bedroom and flopped onto the kline. The blanket was missing but the mattress was soft and the lingering warmth of a home cooked meal lulled him to sleep.

The next time he awoke, the dirty dishware was replaced by another hot meal.

Again and again and again.

If he lurked around the andron—lit a candle to continue that book on balance coins from Era Chrysea, or simply slept on one of those klines instead of the bedroom—it would be easy to catch Mydei the next time he snuck in.

He didn’t. To avoid wasting Mydei’s efforts, he ate everything Mydei left on the low table but promptly disappeared into the bedroom again, sure to lock the door behind him.

All signs of life outside of total darkness were locked outside his sealed windows and blackout curtains. But Mydei brought meals three times a day and time began to hinge on the sorts of food he found waiting.

Breakfast mostly consisted of freshly baked breads flavoured with various herbs or dried fruits. Once or twice there was a stack of honeycakes.

Lunch was also a light meal. Different bread from the morning loaf, and accompanied by soft goats cheese, olives or figs. Sometimes there were chunks of grilled fish, meat or vegetable skewers, cooked to perfection with a charred flavour whilst preserving a softer texture.

Dinner was the heaviest meal and the one with the most variety. Hearty stews and soups of all assortments: different broth bases from pork to fish, and generously layered with legumes, vegetables and quail or hen eggs; spit-roasted meats served over breads that had absorbed all its flavourings; baked pies stuffed full to bursting with meat and herbs.

After the first few meals, he managed to force himself awake long enough to rinse the breakfast cutlery and dishes but retreated to the bedroom before he could drown himself in the sink. By dinner he was only half-asleep at the basin but scrubbed everything reasonably clean before retiring for the night.

Somehow his body became attuned to the opening of the front door, footsteps across the andron, and the close of the front door locking the world out again. While muffled by the door, it was more noise than he was used to Mydei creating, ordinarily prowling like the silent hunter of his epithet. Still, it wasn’t enough to rouse him unless his body wanted to be woken.

The door closed and he clambered out of bed. The sweet smell of honey drizzled over freshly baked cakes wafted into the room before he even opened the door. But there was something new waiting on the low table: a basket beside the tray of food.

When he pulled back the towel draped overtop, a floral aroma rose from neatly folded swathes of fabric. It unravelled when he picked it up. Fresh clothes.

His own tunic was so rumpled he feared the creases would never come out. He couldn’t recall the last time he had changed his garments.

A note was left at the bottom of the basket and he squinted through the dark to read the deliberate, neat lines of ink.

Leave dirty clothes in here.

Oh. It should have been humiliating, and the part of himself that remembered how it felt to be the deliverer squirmed, but he only squinted harder like the words would change. Mydei had already come and gone from the house at his discretion, even if they hadn’t encountered each other yet, there was no hiding the state of everything.

He should have bathed before changing from his sweaty, oily garments into the fresh ones. But that required fetching the firewood from the storage room, waiting for the water to warm through, and then scrubbing himself with soaps and oils when he knew it was futile because he would never again be clean.

The paper pinched between his fingers shook with the tremors of his hand. There was ink and a reed pen on his desk. It would be simple to write a reply without being exposed to Mydei’s sharp eyes, sharp lips, sharp jaw—everything about him so sharp yet so gentle.

Stop. Leave me alone.

Thank you for taking care of me.

Or the one that gripped his chest and squeezed like it meant to wrench his heart out through his ribs.

Sorry for being a burden. 
For being less than you believed I was. 

The note slipped from his fingers to the bottom of the basket where he found it and he bundled his dirty clothes on top. Once he finished eating—honeycakes and yogurt with diced figs—he washed the dishware and left them where he found them beside the basket.

Three meals a day. Every second day, breakfast came with a change of clothes. Initially brand new ones, until the new became old as they were washed and returned to him to rewear.

It was a routine, one his mind allowed him to fall into with little protest, which meant he should have been prepared for what he would find when he left his room for dinner.

But the entire room was alight in the gentle, warm hues of dusk. Curtains drawn back to allow the sinking sun to reach across the room and find refuge in its corners. The long drapes swayed with the cool breeze that entered hesitantly and then all at once through the open windows.

It was the scent of Okhema. Sun-bleached stones, a passing rain he had failed to hear, and the lingered aroma of food cooked in the marketplace. And he finally realised how stagnant the air had been now that it was swept out through the window.

It was as though the entire house remembered how to breathe and he took a deep breath with it.

Once he finished eating and cleaning up, it was time for him to sleep again. But he paused beside the kline.

A thin layer of dust had settled atop that book on Era Chrysea balance coins. He dragged his finger down the cover and it came away grey, so he swiped the bottom of his tunic over the front instead. Then took it with him to the smaller kline by the window.

The dusk was a little dim but he glanced once at the reading candle—wax melted down and wick blackened from the flicker of a flame extinguished in a single puff of air—and he rolled to face the window. He curled up and the dregs of sunlight showed mercy when they illuminated the pages, split open to continue where he left off.

The low light tired his eyes faster than usual. After only a few chapters, he was asleep.

When he woke up, it was to the morning sun glaring into his eyes and the blanket folded over the seat’s curve now draped over him. He jerked upright and only scrambled for the book when it should have already hit the floor. It wasn’t on the mattress with him, but on the side table.

The tassel of his bookmark hung roughly where he recalled reading to, but he had been too stubborn to mark the page and end the night before he reached the chapter’s end. His body relented before his mind, as usual.

His heart pulsed so quickly his head spun with the sound of it in his ears. There was only one person who would have gone to the effort but he still glanced so slowly over his shoulder as though he could be mistaken.

Breakfast was on the table beside a vase of fresh flowers.

Mydei saw him. Mydei saw him.

The only times Mydei had seen him so disgustingly unkempt—greasy hair, crumpled clothes, patchy skin—it was after a long battle where they could both wear such a mess with pride. Not something so pathetic as him locking himself away in his house because—because…

A gentle wind billowed in and lifted a pleasant scent into the air. He thoughtlessly took a deep breath as he naturally sought out that floral tinge. In the vase upon the low table, lilies and hyacinths flourished in the morning sun as the early breeze stirred their sweet scents.

Those flowers. That vase.

The kind Hyacine used to cheer up patients.

His stomach churned and his hand flew to his mouth before. His legs tangled in the blanket as he tried to stand and he kicked it away, stumbling towards the low table as the fresh air was sucked from the room and replaced with that suffocatingly stagnant atmosphere from before.

A sheet of parchment with ink he recognised from his desk was slapped at the centre of the table. Still wet.

Don’t overthink. It was just me.

His knees gave out and he collapsed. He almost laughed but he could close his eyes and force every breath that tried to escape harsh and ragged, almost a dry heave. His elbows slammed against the table and his hands scraped through his matted hair.

Too well. Mydei really knew him too well. Now more than ever.

That was part of the issue.

33,550,336 lifetimes all clamouring for his attention. Did he kiss Mydei for the first time in some ruins ravaged by the black tide? In the empty Hero’s Baths after a close spar? In the dirt of the training grounds after pinning him to the floor with skill and dirty tricks?

Yes. Yes to all of them and more.

Lifetimes where they were too wary of the inevitable end to address the mounting feelings between them. Lifetimes where they were reckless enough, caught in an adrenaline filled moment, to do it anyway. Lifetimes where he returned the ring of Mydei’s mother to his finger with his own hand and a vow to stay by his side.

Lifetimes that all ended the same way.

Dawnmaker pierced through the weakness Mydei entrusted to him alone. Golden blood spilling down red tattoos and skin bared like armour until it soaked the earth. A body and soul that defied Death finally forced into its inescapable grasp with his own hand wrapped around a tenth thoracic vertebra, not with care but to shatter it to dust.

Every whisper of affection and demonstration of love and declaration of forever was accompanied by the memories of someone who was and was not him.

Lurking as a shadow behind something that should have been his but he had forfeited long ago. Heart entombed with grief and still chipped with longing for when it was him. His hands, his arms, his lips no longer able to cherish that immortal body, only destroy it to burn on the pyre and fuel his impossible mission.

Over and over again.

He didn’t leave his bedroom. Not when morning came with the open of his front door, a long pause where Mydei must have seen dinner still untouched on the table, and then the jostle of dishware before the door shut again.

Lunch. Dinner. Breakfast, lunch, dinner again. Then again.

The door remained locked at his hunched back and limbs as numb as his mind. Eyes closed but not blessed with darkness; only cursed with the hitch of breath as Dawnmaker pierced flesh, the hoarse question of how or perhaps why, the final spasms of a body so used to dying yet never like this—everything drenched in the splatter of gold.

The front door opened again and he blinked a bleary eye open. Exactly twenty footsteps to the low table. The clatter of the tray being placed down, which should have been followed with the jostle of uneaten dinner being lifted. Then twenty footsteps back to the front door.

There was no reason for the footsteps to be getting louder.

His muscles tensed and his eyes widened, senses discarding everything except the footsteps that had since gone silent right at his back. As though this were a fight—a simple threat he could cut down with a single swing of his greatsword.

But his muscles were weak and spasmed at the sudden use, so unlike the lethargic haze they had settled into with his mind. There was no battlefield or grand purpose. He was curled up on the cold, dark floor of his bedroom with his back to the door. Locked when Mydei jostled the handle.

“Deliv—Phainon.”

A shudder wracked through him at that deep drawl of his name. The lilt of it he could feel right against the shell of his ear, heedless of the barrier he forced between them.

“Open the door.”

To obey or flee he wasn’t certain but he was already on his hands and knees before he stopped himself.

A rap of metal knuckles against wood. “I can hear you breathing. Now open the door.”

His body stilled down to his breath.

“Have it your way,” Mydei said gruffly but he could have sworn there was a hint of amusement, the type that curled the edge of Mydei’s lip while he denied he was smiling. “This is your one warning: move.”

Why? But his tongue was stuck dry to the roof of his mouth.

A few measured steps away. Then a rapid approach and he threw himself out the way just as Mydei kicked the door straight from the frame.

Sunlight flooded in and he flinched away, eyes burning as he lowered them to the floor. The only place he could look was the seam where the fallen door met the floor. Even once the light dimmed behind a long shadow, he didn’t lift his gaze.

Slow footsteps across the fallen wood. The kind someone used when approaching a feral animal. It was apt. He felt on the edge of snapping his teeth.

He didn’t. Everything was sluggish, from his muscles to his mind, rendering him unable to move at all, let alone quick enough to catch flesh between fangs.

In front of him, Mydei’s shoes stopped. “Phainon, lift your head.”

Everything was too loud in his skull. Too complicated and tangled in his chest. If any of that deciphered into a desire to look, to meet Mydei’s eye and let him witness the unsalvageable thing he had wasted so much time on, he still refrained.

Mydei sighed. Then lowered himself to one knee.

His head jerked away on wild instinct but Mydei snagged his jaw between metal claws. Faster than he remembered, or maybe he was just slower. There was nothing for him to do: no strength left to fight and nowhere to go. He relented to the tip of his head back.

Eyes gold and slitted, creased with smug satisfaction. Lips pulled into a small smirk exposing the pointed tip of his teeth. Hair the hues of sunset across a horizon leaning towards him alone as Mydei dipped across that small distance between them.

Mydei’s smirk grew but his voice was nowhere near as sharp when he said, “There you are.”

His breath hitched and he exhaled the tension from his muscles. He almost slumped fully to the ground but Mydei’s grip on his chin kept his head up and back arched.

When Mydei released his chin, it was to straighten and offer the same hand; black leather glove over his palm, soft and unscarred underneath, and polished gauntlet deadly over his smooth and uncalloused fingers. “Now come eat.”

Although Mydei had barged his way in and trapped him in place, that outstretched hand waited for him.

His fingers curled tight against the ground but he inhaled metal polished in oil and the warmth of kitchen fires, and they unfurled. He entrusted his hand to Mydei.

Mydei led them to the andron and sat himself down. Their hands still joined together didn’t give him much choice but to follow. Once Mydei was absolutely certain he wouldn’t run away and find some other door to hide behind, he let go of his hand.

Mydei jerked his chin towards the tray. “Eat.”

The lift of the dish covers revealed a steaming bowl of porridge topped with figs, pomegranate seeds and honey; yogurt scattered with berries; and unleavened bread on the side.

The bread was… familiar. Not from the many loaves Mydei had previously baked. Not even from the stretch of time Mydei had been providing him three meals a day, nor the lifetimes he spent cooking for the Heirs. But the sight of it and the smell still rattled something loose in the back of his mind.

It wasn’t until the first loaf was between his teeth that the memory fully dislodged and his eyes stung.

Cyrene. Something she used to bake often in the very first cycle. They were both well into adulthood by then—an age she never managed to reach again before the long-awaited arrival of the pale dawn—and far from the small village by the coast where wheat and salt were abundant. But inside Okhema’s walls she learned to recapture the taste of home and often shared it with him.

He sniffled and Mydei leaned forward to take the cloth napkin from the tray. When Mydei saw his dirtied hands, he lifted the napkin himself and gauntlets much too gentle for war dabbed his tears away.

“Phainon,” he said in a hushed voice, “there’s no rush.”

His tears fell swifter and his breath came as a shuddered gasp as he grabbed Mydei’s wrist, begging him with actions when his words were failing him. “Why…”

Mydei waited in silence for him to finish. Eyes as dazzling as the sun never strayed from his. Not the intense glare at the height of summer, but a sun meant to illuminate the darkest crevices of night until there was nowhere for him to hide.

“Why do you call me that?” he croaked, hoarse from lack of use and care.

Mydei dragged his thumbs under the curve of his damp eyes, cloth already forgotten and if only the gauntlets would be next so he could feel Mydei’s bare skin. “Be more specific.”

“Phainon,” he gritted out like a curse. It was one in a way. The life lived as a hero only to lose it all. “I’m not…”

The person you fell in love with. Every time.

Mydei kissed his teeth but it wasn’t cutting enough to be reprimanding, serrated edges sanded down into something smooth. “I once told you that I am simply more capable of enduring pain than you. I was wrong. My mind contains the memories of every lifetime from the first until now. You are forced to bear twice as much hardship. The memories of you as the deliverer, and you as the black-robed swordsman.”

The one who was loved and the one who longed to be loved. The one who was surrounded by others and the one who was so terribly lonely. The one who was adored as a hero and the one who was abhorred as a villain.

Mydei lowered the cloth: no longer a shield he could hide his flushed cheeks, red eyes, and snotty nose behind. Much less everything much uglier underneath.

But Mydei still smiled when he cupped his cheek. “If you wish for me to call you something else then give me another name. Until then, I will call you by the name you gave yourself and gave to me. But know that, in my eyes, you have never changed, Phainon.”

Mydei was never one to lie. He was stoic, curt and entirely truthful. A trait that irked many Okhemans who thought it disrespectful to disregard common courtesy and rhetoric. But he always found endearing.

He searched for one anyway. For the barest hint of revulsion so overwhelming even Mydei couldn’t mask it. Nothing.

Only a pleased curl at the corner of his lips because Mydei knew he had him. That he couldn’t avert his eyes any longer from the truth he hadn’t screamed through his door but carefully left on his table for him to find.

No matter how the world tried to restrain him, Mydei lived so unapologetically as himself.

The rest of the meal was taken in silence. Mydei briefly disappeared into the bathroom to light the bathroom furnace but didn’t press for answers even once he returned. Fortunate, since he wasn’t ready to give him one, or even certain if he wanted to contradict him.

While Khaslana was his birth name, it lay abandoned in the remains of his home village. It was the name Phainon that had accompanied him as he wandered Amphoreus and eventually found a home in Okhema. And when everything was reverted to the very beginning and he stood in those golden wheat fields that would be destroyed at his own hands, the name he unearthed and reclaimed was Khaslana.

But he liked being Phainon. It was the name people called when he walked through the marketplace. That children cheered and giggled when he dangled them from his arms or tossed them high to catch them unscathed. That brought the scent of wheat and the sea to sun-bleached stone.

That Mydei whispered for his ears alone.

A name he abandoned when he raised his sword against his home and his second chance at a family.

While Mydei balanced the temperature of the bathwater, he forced himself through the motions of the rest: preparing the towels, gathering a change of clothes, and stripping out of his old ones.

When confronted with his reflection in the bronze mirror for the first time since… before this body became Khaslana, he could hardly meet his own eyes from the shame. It was a miracle Mydei could stand to be anywhere near him. He was disgustingly filthy. Hardly human because and beneath it all.

But Mydei only added a few perfumed drops of oil to the bath, steam blooming with the smell of myrtle, and then arched a brow. A silent question of what he was so preoccupied with he couldn’t get himself in a washbasin. He only shook his head and lowered himself in.

Far from the scorching hot baths, the water temperature was perfect for him and he sighed as it washed over him.

Mydei knelt by the washbasin, head pillowed upon his arms hooked over the edge. He met Mydei’s amused eye once and then sank down until the water was over his lips, staring straight ahead at his tucked knees.

He wasn’t embarrassed to be exposed in front of Mydei. They bathed together twice a day, sometimes more, and had stripped each other naked innumerable times before, for practical reasons like battlefield treatment or not so practical reasons.

But Mydei was squinting at him and that made him more conscious of himself.

Until Mydei opened his hand. “Give me your arm.”

He placed his forearm in Mydei’s grasp before he even finished asking, “Why?”

“You’re filthy,” Mydei answered bluntly and grabbed the soap.

He scrubbed the scented soap into his skin with the pumice stone. When he checked for any signs of discomfort but found them absent, he unleashed his true viciousnesses. He cleaned with the brutal strength and efficiency of a warrior fresh from the battlefield, who didn’t know when he would next find warm water to bathe with: scouring bodily oils and sweat that had accumulated over… he didn’t want to know how long.

Then he lathered his skin with oil and used the strigil to scrape the soap and oil off into one of the two buckets of water beside him.

Once one arm was done, Mydei walked around the washbasin to do the same to the other arm. Then he tugged his leg to hang over the edge and did both of those, but left him to wash his own torso while Mydei cleaned his back.

Afterwards, Mydei tipped his head back and scrubbed his hair with lye soap. He leaned into the touch massaging his scalp with carefully rounded nails and just the right amount of pressure.

“It’s longer,” Mydei remarked mildly, more to fill space and satisfy idle curiosity than delve deep. “Will you trim it?”

A noncommittal hum. “I haven’t thought about it.”

“You could grow it out.”

“I’ve never done that before.”

Mydei shrugged, dragging his nails down to the hairs at the back of his neck. “If you dislike it, then you can trim it. You have time to decide these things.”

A cupped hand hovered over his face and he closed his eyes as Mydei tipped the water, rinsing through his hair. It spilled into the dirty bucket between Mydei’s legs and he scooped another handful from the bucket of clean, lukewarm water to rinse again.

When the water ran clean and another handful didn’t come, he kept his eyes shut. He knew what he would see if he opened them: the bathroom ceiling cast in the flickering firelight of the furnace, Mydei hovering above him with his usual terse expression that his face rested in whenever he wasn’t actively smiling, frowning or scowling.

A defence as natural to him as that undying body and one Phainon easily sidestepped. Not to harm him but to satiate the need to see what lay underneath that demeanour of a warrior prince. Then ask him why he bothered to hide something so lovely even when he was greedy to keep it for himself. 

He  needed a moment in the dark, warm and floating, to breathe and speak quietly, “Mydei.”

“What?”

“Why are you…” he struggled to find the right word, years upon years of education failing him, “inconveniencing yourself like this? You must have better things to do with your time considering the changes Amphoreus has undergone. You could be anywhere doing anything—even somewhere beyond the starry sky.”

A sharp breath, held in, and his skin prickled. Not only because it was scrubbed raw but because he knew he’d said the wrong thing after all.

As if to make up for all the silence he had condemned himself to, he couldn’t stop himself from continuing, “It must take a lot of time to purchase the ingredients and prepare these meals. Not to mention the laundry. Surely the Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos has more important tasks to be undertaking now that the black tide has receded and his citizens likely want to return home.

“Or perhaps you could join the Astral Express. If you asked the Trailblazer, they would certainly welcome you aboard. You possess plenty of experience with wandering after all. You may enjoy the sights of things we never could have even imagined. But make sure to write me then if you do.”

In the short pause where he needed to take a breath, Mydei interjected flatly, “Are you done?”

Timidly, eyes still tightly shut, he nodded.

Mydei heaved a sigh and those fingers returned to his hair. Not to lather soap but to massage his scalp all the same. “First of all, discard the idea that this is an inconvenience to me. In all the time that you’ve known me, have I ever let myself be feebly forced into anything?”

That was a lot of time to search through. But there was no need when he already knew the answer. He shook his head.

“Everything I do, I do because it’s the path that I’ve chosen for myself. Nothing more.” 

“But…” He clenched his hands at his sides.

“My time and my efforts are my own. Only I can decide how they’re put to use, and who is deserving of them.”

Phainon laughed, breathy and low, dissipating like the steam off the water. To use a word like deserve—Mydei knew him too well indeed.

“As for the rest of your answer,” Mydei paused, so uncharacteristic for that unerring confident drawl that Phainon’s eyes opened. Mydei startled as their eyes met and he glanced away, cheeks red from more than the heated bathroom. “We can discuss it another time.”

Alone, he dried himself off and dressed in a clean tunic. Upon exiting the bathroom, he realised what Mydei had done and chuckled. His bedroom door had been propped up against the frame.

He shook his head, a smile tugging at his lips, and turned to search the house for wherever Mydei had gone to next. But the crack of light between the door and the frame caught his eye and pulled him in like an insect towards self-annihilation.

Mydei had very earnestly attempted to stand it back up despite being completely much beyond repair. He was lucky the frame hadn’t ripped and brought the wall down with it considering Mydei’s kicks had shattered Titankin.

A cursory inspection confirmed it was beyond salvaging with his own meagre woodworking skills, limited to carving lumpy statues if he were honest. So he picked it up and moved it aside entirely, propping it against the wall and exposing the room to the rest of the house.

The curtains and windows were open. On the cabinet beside the kline was a vase of lilies and hyacinths.

Phainon spun towards the rest of the house. He could have sworn he heard Mydei in the kitchen.

“I disposed of all your rotten food and cleared out your icebox,” Mydei informed him as he washed the dishware, quick and factual. Like a mission report and not charity.

Phainon waited for the lurch in his chest and pulse in his ears, shame crushingly heavy yet his like a shackle on a criminal. But his face only warmed slightly, barely noticeable when it was still dewy from the bath. The weight was less than he remembered and he shifted his stance to carry it better. 

“Ah. I didn’t realise,” he admitted with a scratch at the back of his head. “You’re very efficient, Mydei. I take my eye off you for a moment and you accomplish so much. Here, let me finish up.”

Mydei eyed him sceptically but he shook his hands dry and stepped aside. “Do what you want.”

While Phainon finished cleaning the dishware, Mydei leaned his back against the counter, arms crossed and gaze flitting between the distant window across the house and Phainon.

He knew because every time Phainon snuck a glance himself, their eyes met and they stared, daring the other to look away first. It was always Phainon, who needed to focus on the dishware before he sliced his palm open on the knife still somewhere in the water.

A silence lingered between them. In their small gestures and raised eyebrows and curled lips. It was comfortable. The morning sunlight and breeze was crisp in the air with the scent of sweet flowers. He felt more at ease than he had since he first locked out the rest of the world on his doorstep.

With the tray packed and the basket of laundry in Mydei’s hands, there was no reason to remain any longer but they both lingered by the front door. Uncertain what to say next when they were both hesitant to part ways or ask to stay.

“Would you mind passing my gratitude to Cyrene?” Phainon finally settled on. “And Hyacine. For the bread and flowers.”

Mydei nodded and tapped the front of his sandals against the ground, sliding them fully into place as he prepared to leave. “I’ll see you for lunch.”

“It’s a date.”

It slipped out like a bad habit and hung between them like a noose Phainon had tied himself. But when he swallowed without recanting his slip of the tongue, Mydei smiled.

Not a sly, victorious curl of his lips or a smug smirk. A sincere smile. A fondness Phainon thought he would never be privy to again.

“It’s a date,” Mydei promised.

When the door closed behind him, there was no dread, no guilt, at the knowledge he would be back. If anything, Phainon longed for him to return sooner as he sat at the window to continue his book, hand idly twirling the ends of his hair and wondering how it would feel long.

From then on, all the meals Mydei brought through the door were for two. Since the house call was extended with their shared meal and conversation, Mydei opted to bring a heavier breakfast, forgo lunch entirely, and return for dinner.

Now that daylight cycled through the house, the restlessness began to creep up on him. He no longer passed the hours with sleep: he thoroughly tidied his bedroom, with Mydei’s help and no judgement when Phainon failed to finish before Mydei arrived with dinner; polished his small antique weapons collection and Mydei admired their new sheen when he came searching for Phainon in the decorative armoury; completed his book on Era Chrysea balance coins and another on Era Bellica vases.

He was halfway through a book on differentiating Kremnoan weaponry from Mountain Dweller crafts from fakes, when Mydei brought dinner and another surprise. 

Phainon frowned at the basket reserved for laundry Mydei wordlessly set atop Phainon’s outstretched legs. Then down at his tunic.

It was fresh. Mydei had begun to return washed garments in bulk and trusted Phainon to not need the reminder every three days.

His attempt to catch Mydei’s eye, brows creased with his unspoken question, were futile. Mydei’s back was to him as he unpacked the basket of food, more convenient to carry than a tray now that he was transporting meals for two everyday, on the usual low table.

Phainon put his book aside and reached into the basket. The first brush of fabric against his fingers and he knew that only one person in Okhema tailored garments from such fine fabrics.

When he lifted it and let the clothing unravel every new detail confirmed his suspicions. The beautiful gold embroidered leaves and laurels. The stitchings of the fabric to accentuate the waist and arms. The garments fitted to his exact measurements.

The craftsmanship could belong to no one except Aglaea.

There were multiple garments inside the basket. So many that, once unfurled from their precision folds, it was difficult to believe they had ever fit inside. Chitons and tunics, trousers and shirts, coats long or short.

None of them resembled the outfit he had spent lifetimes wearing for the sake of appearances. The friendly face of the Flame Chase, easy to recognise in any crowd and ask for help with the smallest of issues.

Considering he had abandoned more modest ideas of propriety long ago, and his bedroom still lacked a functional door, he drew the curtains and changed clothes in the andron with Mydei sat upon the kline as he decanted their drinks.

A sweeping white chiton adorned with the same gold patterns that Aglaea herself wore. A trailing blue decorative chlamys over his shoulder. A golden vambrace made for peace and not war, decorated with a blazing sun warming the vines and laurels.

Their meals laid out, Mydei reclined against the curved end. The image of a king at leisure as he sipped his chalice of pomegranate juice and milk, watching the entertainment.

Which happened to be Phainon twirling in his new clothes like a dancing girl. “What do you think?”

He rumbled a low laugh and swirled his chalice. “Do you except me to insult the craft of the Goldweaver herself?”

Phainon pursed his lips. That wasn’t a compliment. He could admit it wasn’t his usual attire—too fancy, too impractical—and that his body wasn’t quite as it once was. Not because it was weathered and cracked open but because his muscle mass had declined with his activity.

But the fabric draped over him like a benevolent embrace. He wasn’t certain if it was wool or linen, although at least one of the garments from the basket was most certainly silk, but Aglaea only used materials of the highest quality and it was abundantly clear when it brushed his skin. Beneath his nose, was the scent of Aglaea’s favourite bath oil she frequently dropped into the Hero’s Bath.

Mydei leaned forward to set his chalice down and huffed a laugh, thick and sweet like the honey he generously dolloped on Phainon’s food. “It suits you. You should indulge in finer things more often.”

His mind was still caught on that little laugh and the rest of his words did nothing to help. “Oh. I thought… it must be strange for me to be wearing such things.”

A village boy. A wanderer. Then a man of the people.

“Not at all. I gifted you finer things in the past,” Mydei said as nonchalantly as everything else whilst he uncovered his dinner.

Silk sheets and robes dyed resplendent rich reds and blues. Gold jewellery inlaid with red gemstones larger than even Mydei’s blue ones. Antique books, Kremnoan weaponry. If the world still worked like Mydei’s days in exile then Phainon had no doubt Mydei would have laid city-states at his feet.

He hadn’t forgotten all those things shared between them. Even at the point in every cycle he forgot more than he remembered, moved with instinct more than thought, he always yearned for it.

He simply hadn’t let himself think at length about those lifetimes lived in something like bliss.

Now that they combined to assail him, his face heated and he swayed, dumbly taking his seat before he could collapse into a pile steaming not from the millions of flames inside him—but from embarrassment.

Mydei didn’t comment. He simply tore into his meal with a ravenous hunger after Phainon had kept him waiting.

Only a day passed before Mydei waltzed into the house with the meal basket dangled from his elbow and something else balanced atop the crook of each arm. Phainon jumped from the kline and left his book—a new one on the evolution of paintings designs on clay pots throughout the Chrysos Wars—to alleviate Mydei of the cumbersome looking burdens.

They were big and round yet so light they swayed when he kicked the door closed behind him, ready to tumble the moment Mydei’s balance was the slightest bit off centre.

Although, even if they tumbled and smack the hard floors, they were all fabric and stuffing. Round bodies, four legs, pointed tails, big smiles with even bigger eyes. One of them even had two horns.

At Mydei’s flat look, Phainon stopped eyeing the stuffed dolls and jolted back to action, scooping both into his arms. He examined them again while Mydei kicked off his sandals, then followed him deeper into the house.

“Are these chimeras?” Phainon asked but the answer was obvious. “Have you developed a taste for children’s toys?”

Mydei scoffed. “Castorice made them.”

It certainly was her chosen weave, soft to the touch but sturdy enough to withstand a number of strong hugs. Stuffed full with no expense spared and seamlessly closed. There was an intricacy to the added details, of someone who mimicked Aglaea’s needlework, not to the same level but was certainly practiced.

It was rare for any Castorice to share this particular hobby, even more secretive than her writing. But Phainon had always been overjoyed the times she felt comfortable enough to overcome her embarrassment and trust him.

Phainon lifted one higher, the muted orange one, and squinted from its silly smile to the man over its shoulder. “This one looks like you.”

Mydei opened the food basket. “She claimed the same. The grey one reminded her of you when she was visiting the chimeras in the Garden.”

The one with crooked horns to match its smile, even sillier than the orange one yet so much more mischievous. So Castorice could see such a harmless little thing and still think of Phainon.

Phainon hummed. “I think she’s mistaken.” Mydei’s brows furrowed and his lips parted to argue. But Phainon poked the cheek of the orange chimera and continued, “You’re much cuter.”

Now Mydei’s lips were parted to gape soundlessly. Then his cheeks flushed the same colour as the ends of his hair and he swiftly turned away.

Phainon laughed. Laughed. From deep in his gut where this sound had been bottled away for so long that his body had almost forgotten. Now that it remembered, it refused to stop until the ache in his stomach and lungs almost brought him to his knees. He salvaged a scrap of his dignity by flopping face first onto the kline instead of the floor.

“It wasn’t that funny, haikas,” Mydei berated, just loud enough for Phainon to hear over his cackles and face buried in the cushioning.

When he calmed enough to take a deep breath, he lifted his head. Mydei was already staring at him, eyes creased not with indignation but tenderness.

Phainon laughed again and it was more hysterical than before, yet more fragile for it. His stomach ached but it felt like relief when Mydei joined him even though neither of them could name what exactly they were laughing at.

So Phainon was alert for the unexpected whenever Mydei walked through the door. Even so, the next surprise wasn’t immediately obvious when Mydei came for breakfast. It was only once Phainon opened the basket with the intent to unpack did he find the sheafs of parchment tied tight with twine and stacked atop the food.

That penmanship. He may have been a little snarky more often than not, but he was still an attentive student who diligently read all Anaxa’s feedback, no matter how acrid on the surface, and took it in stride. It was a chance to improve himself offered in glaring red ink.

His hands gripped the pages tight enough to crease. “What is it?”

Mydei reached past him to lift the porridge from the basket. “Do you see my name on that?”

“I suppose not,” Phainon mumbled absentmindedly as he skimmed the title. A research proposal into… “So, one could say, you’re just the deliverer.”

Mydei didn’t dignify that with a response but he made direct eye contact as he loudly slurped from his chalice. Phainon couldn’t fault him for it and sat without his usual teasing push for, at least, a pity laugh. 

While they ate, Mydei didn’t comment on how Phainon was too preoccupied with Anaxa’s writings to act as a proper conversation partner. If he genuinely thought the breach in etiquette was rude then he would have made a blunt remark but he seemed to enjoy the silence as he ate.

It was a research proposal into Phainon. An investigation into the mental and physical properties that allowed him to sustain so many Coreflames for such a prolonged period when a Chrysos Heir could only hold one before it consumed them. How his mind processed so many memories. The long-term side-effects of such an endeavour. The potential treatment or aids that could be beneficial.

While his body was of no consequence, the thought of being the subject of such experiments—of his every thought and feeling over millions of years being pried apart for observation…

“Mydei?” Phainon called hesitantly and he hummed around a mouthful of honeyed porridge. “Do you recall Anaxa’s experiments on you?”

Mydei swallowed. “Of course. My mind doesn’t have a hole in it.”

The number of cycles where Anaxa and Mydei never met was disproportionately high compared to other Heirs that lived in the same time frame. Or perhaps not so surprising considering Anaxa’s distaste towards leaving the Grove and Mydei’s lack of enrolment there.

But every cycle they met resulted in some kind of research into Mydei’s body. Anaxa sought to recreate the effects of his immortality in other living beings. Unfortunately, dunking them into the Sea of Souls only resulted in a few dead rats. Attempts to alchemically simulate Mydei’s regenerative capabilities were also without success, unless monsters almost as frightening as the black tide was success.

It was also an opportunity to learn the mechanisms behind the Sea of Souls. Anytime Mydei ended up there, he collected data no matter how irrelevant it seemed and passed it along until Anaxa’s laboratory and library were filled with notes.

Phainon swallowed and fiddled with his spoon. “Was there no discomfort on your part?”

Mydei chewed thoughtfully, giving himself time to carefully consider before he answered. “If there was, I would have had no qualms telling that man. He may be pushy if he thinks he’s on the trail of answers, but he was diligent and planned rigorously to avoid serious harm. Besides, it would have been a great boon to the Flame Chase if he got any results. And to myself.”

These were all things he already knew about Anaxa from years of tutelage. One lifetime would have been enough when, even more than Mydei, who was constrained by the chains of old grudges and kingship, his eccentric professor lived life on his own terms. Honest and unyielding in his pursuit of knowledge.

“That is helpful to know,” Phainon admitted, somehow more reassured when it was from Mydei than his own mind and memories. “I’ll consider it.”

Between breakfast and dinner, Phainon paced around the room with the research proposal in hand. It was a brilliant idea.

In theory.

In practice it meant being poked and prodded and gouged open. His memories, his experiences, his deteriorating mental state almost as bad as the body held together by sheer force of will.

The martyrdom, the dead humanity, the god complex Anaxa had pointedly deduced through one conversation. The reason he levelled a gun against him, not as an unruly student who needed discipline but as a monster that needed to be put down. He may have been hurt, or maybe he was already too numb even the first time to feel more than annoyance at the rebellion.

His body wasn’t as fragile now as it had been then, or any time since the first few cycles. He was intimately familiar with a healthy body suddenly strained to the breaking point, transformed into something one strong wind away from crumbling to ash. Ever since the arrival of the true dawn, his body felt sturdy and steady.

Normal.

But his mind…

It was one misstep away from being snuffed out again. He knew it. One wrong word, or bad reminder, and there was no telling what he would do. The Coreflames were still in that space hollowed inside his chest where he discarded the heart that used to live there to let the flames ravage him from the inside out.

Light glinted into his eye and he winced away from his thoughts. He searched for the source and found it on the side table beside the window. Something small and shiny, reflecting the daylight into a harsh glare when the sun sank low enough to come through his window onto the table at just the right angle.

He placed the parchment down and pinched the coin between his thumb and index finger. It was warm from the sun when he flipped it between his fingers, as though the design would change in a blink.

A coin of whimsy. Three letters scratched into the otherwise flawless surface: IOU.

The window wasn’t big enough for even the most lithe cat to sneak inside but he didn’t question how it landed on his side table. He simply breathed a shaky exhale and laid the coin over the research proposal.

He returned to his bedroom to lay down, stealing the plushie of Honey Fruitcake from Beagle Coconut so he could hug it close to his chest.

Cifera was always elusive. A consequence of the enormous burden she chose to shoulder: the Dawn Device itself. They rarely ever shared a particularly close relationship.

Sometimes they would chance upon each other on expeditions far from Okhema—from Aglaea, whose perception through lies and trickery Cifera feared most. Other times she would stop by the holy city just long enough to sow some mischief and catch a glimpse of the people she longed to be close to.

They were alike and yet couldn’t be further apart. Scorned as a thief who sacrificed themselves to become a hero. Praised as a hero who fell from grace into a villain.

Phainon rolled out of bed, shuffled back to the andron, and returned to bed with the research papers on his cabinet and the coin warm in his palm.

Dinner the next day was followed with a game of chess.

“I wasn’t aware you understood such intellectual games,” Phainon remarked cheerily while they set up the board.

Mydei rolled his eyes but all the black pieces on his side of the board stood in their proper places. “Chess isn’t so different from battle.”

Phainon chuckled and pushed another white pawn into place. “If I knew, I would have challenged you ages ago.”

“You only have yourself to blame for believing otherwise.”

One more piece. He reached into the pouch. Then frowned. He waved his hand, feeling along the edges, but groped only air.

“Mydei, you could have just said you never intended to play fairly.”

“Insulting my honour? It’s as though you see your imminent demise and wish to change our battleground to something more physical.”

He would very much not wish for that considering they were inside his house but Mydei had thrown down the gauntlet and Phainon could never concede once he did.

“I could say the same to you,” he protested and lifted his pouch into clear sight, tipping it upside down with a shake. “My side has lost its king before the battle even began.”

Realisation slackened Mydei’s features that had been honing themselves for a skirmish. He dug through his pockets and placed a slim wooden box into Phainon’s palm. Heavy, but it made little noise when he rattled it.

Inside was a king’s chess piece. Transparent except for the light thrown about inside. He might have thought it were shaped from glass if it weren’t for the considerable weight and scintillation of light inside.

He poked the surrounding cushioning, almost afraid to ask. “Is this…”

“Diamond,” Mydei confirmed as he studied the board still not yet in play.

The weight grew heavier. He carefully set it down on the board before his hands could sweat so much it slipped and scuffed against the floor. It was almost too big for its square, and the sunlight bounced through, casting coloured shards over the board.

The design was similar to one he had seen in the past. On the other side of the board. The colouration was different but the size, shape and cut of the body and crown were the same. Cerydra’s king piece with a final noticeable difference: the sun carved onto the face.

He cleared his throat. “The cut and clarity are very impressive.”

That one chunk of diamond could probably buy up half the city.

Mydei crossed his arms. “Are you going to begin, or keep delaying the inevitable?”

“Perhaps I simply want to savour the process of my own victory,” he goaded but moved his first pawn to the sound of Mydei’s scoff.

Mydei played chess with the same ruthless attention to detail he demonstrated in battle. He scanned the terrain for strengths and weaknesses, accruing them into a strategy. He wove together obfuscations and his direct moves, so Phainon was never certain if he understood Mydei’s full strategy and had countered or simply played into it.

Still, it was Phainon’s victory. Mydei raised his chalice to toast his success and Phainon clinked them together before throwing back the rest of his drink.

The chess board became another part of their routine. Not every day, but a few times a week they went back and forth to trade victory and defeat claimed with inanimate objects instead of flesh and blood.

It was an in-between day. Mydei came for dinner but they had no other plans, yet Phainon invited him to the table by the window, no chessboard in sight, and he took one of the klines.

Mydei swiftly grew bored of Phainon’s pestering to see the progress on his enlarged teleslate and moved to sit beside him. An arm thrown over the seat’s curve, Phainon had a clear view over Mydei’s shoulder to the glowing teleslate and placed his book—a collection of epic poetry from Aidonia—aside to watch Mydei draw.

He squinted at the chimeras onscreen, standing very dramatically opposite one another as they prepared to duel in front of the setting sun. “Are those us?”

“All good artists take inspiration from their real life experiences.”

“I don’t recall ever consenting to you using my likeness.”

“Take it up with Talanton. I’ll see you in the courts.”

The stage had been set for their usual back and forth jabs. The potential arguments rushed through his thoughts with a mind suddenly sharpened back to that of a debate champion.

A sound drifted through the open window and every argument in his mind quieted. Still, like the air in his lungs. Waiting.

The sound came again. A string instrument. Played not with fingers but a bow.

Every note flowed like the ocean’s waves into a beautiful melody. One that trilled through his muscles and hummed in his veins. It seeped into his skull, pushing against the edges where his mind wandered far from his own reach, and washing away every impurity.

It was yearning and pride and triumph.

A final strong note rang out and then silence fell. A beat passed. Applause and cheers rose up from the city streets.

Only one person could play such a mesmerising piece. Hysilens. So close she must have been on the rooftops nearby.

Although silence had returned outside, once again settling like the dusk over day, the music looped through Phainon’s head and came out as a low hum. Mydei’s head bobbed along as he drew until he finished and played the short animation for Phainon to watch.

A couple of days later, when someone knocked at the door, Phainon didn’t hesitate when he reached to open it. Although Mydei had the key, perhaps his hands were too full to open the door himself.

No one was there. Only a small box left in a basket of sunflowers on his doorstop.

Seated in the andron again, he found a folded note tucked in the ribbon tied into a neat bow.

He knew the handwriting and he traced every slope and curve once, twice, almost a third time before he finally swallowed and pulled the ribbon free. Without it, the lid popped off easily.

A thin rectangle of gold crowned in red.

He was so preoccupied staring that he didn’t hear the front door open and footsteps until it was too late.

It was only a gift from the Trailblazer and their friends. Simply because it was handed to him in invitation didn’t mean anything. It would make a decent decoration on his desk for him to smile at whenever he saw and remembered the hero who had come to save him.

But when Mydei loomed over the table and his eyes caught on the boarding pass to the Astral Express, a train across the stars to the furthest reaches of the universe, far from Amphoreus, something complicated passed across his face. Then disappeared behind a stonewall.

And Phainon’s promise that it would stay in its box disappeared too.

Neither of them addressed it through breakfast or dinner. That day nor the next.

Because Mydei would never burden him by asking him to stay or telling him to leave. A man who valued actions over words, his refusal to confront it head on without prompting was meant to tell Phainon one thing: the decision was wholly his to make.   

It had gone straight into his bedroom where it was out of sight during Mydei’s visits. Not as Mydei discussed the poor selection of produce in the market that morning. Not as Phainon succinctly summarised the legacies captured in the stars, now that they had returned to Amphoreus for all to see.

The food tasted different on Phainon’s tongue. Not bad just… like something was missing. It must have shown on his face but Mydei didn’t blame the produce or anything else. He simply glanced away.

The curtains and windows were open. Fresh lilies and hyacinths bloomed on the table. The meal was warm and filling.

So why did everything feel so stagnant again.

It was Phainon. It had to be. There was no one to blame but himself. He was stagnant, had been for a length of time he refused to consider, like someone already dead. A ghost haunting this house.

As he lay on his side in the bedroom with the Astral Express ticket, cold and thin yet so solid it felt unbreakable, illuminated by the moonlight in his palm, he considered. Sometimes large changes were needed to break out of a slump.

It would be a complete change. The Trailblazer and Dan Heng would know him, of course, and the rest of the crew only knew of him due to their intervention in Amphoreus and the stories from their two stranded crew members.

But it would be a chance to shed his past in exchange for a new future. He could take a new name: the burden of Phainon, Khaslana, the Deliverer would no longer be his to bear.

He could run away. Nothing more than the coward he had already proven himself to be when he couldn’t even bring himself to leave his house. To be perceived by all those who had placed their faith in him and been disappointed. More than that. Harmed, by the very hands they had entrusted to herald the dawn.

He would never have to see the same coldness Aglaea reserved for the Council now turned upon him where she had once gazed at him with motherly warmth.

Hyacine’s sorrow at the old friend, already beyond all recognition and salvation, she could never lend a healing hand.

Cyrene’s grief at the husk of her childhood friend, hollowed out to nothing over the years of a plan they had concocted together.

Castorice’s agony at the soul she could never bring to peaceful rest, but instead succumbed to herself.

Anaxa’s disdain at the waylaid student who had lost all reason and spiralled towards insanity.

Cifera’s disgust at the applauded hero who wasn’t so heroic after all and fell from grace so easily.

Cerydra’s distrust of someone who was more foe than friend, never to be trusted even as a mere pawn.

Hysilens’ skepticism of the convictions behind his blade and his ability to wield it.

Tribbios divided into three who gazed up at him with childlike wonder and disbelief yet guided him as a teacher.

All these people who had become more than friends or family to him. They were inextricably connected in ways that went beyond life and death. But those threads were also bloodied and tangled by his own hands.

And yet…

Aglaea, who had tailored him all sorts of new garments.

Hyacine, who brightened his home with flowers.

Cyrene, who reproduced the taste of home just for him.

Castorice, who gave him company in the form of soft plushies.

Anaxa, who wanted to mitigate the worst of the consequences from his own actions.

Cifera, who thought he was worthy of a calling upon her for a favour.

Cerydra, who honoured him as the final piece standing that successfully kept the game in play until defeat became victory.

Hysilens, who called the oceans forth to perform a song just for him.

Tribbie, Trianne and Trinnon, who dropped a carefully sealed tube into the basket alongside dinner. Seated on the kline so the barest space remained between their shoulders, Mydei let Phainon open it and unfurl the parchment inside.

A coloured drawing. All the Chrysos Heirs together in a field of sunflowers under a shining sun and a message:

We all miss you, Snowy!

All of them. Every single one of them.

Mydei who witnessed him at his highest highs and his lowest lows and still earnestly declared that Phainon had never changed. That he was still the very same person Mydei had chosen to love and cherish.

And he proved it every day even when it was rotten work.

It wasn’t a vow they had exchanged in every lifetime. But it was always buried in their hearts as a promise that they meant even if it wasn’t sealed with a kiss or a ring.

This was another lifetime. One they could share without fear, without knowing beyond doubt, that it would all crumble around them at the end.

“I love you.”

That small final distance between them closed as Phainon threw himself forwards and into Mydei’s arms that had been waiting  so patiently for him all along. Ones that had taken care of him so tenderly without asking anything in return.

“I love you,” Phainon breathed and he laughed at the words he, perhaps, was never worthy of saying in the first place. But back then and also now, he said it anyway, “I love you. I love you. Mydei, I love you more than anything.”

Mydei’s arms wrapped around him and tugged him close, taking Phainon with him when he leaned back to lay them down. So Phainon’s face was tucked under his chin and against his jugular, thrumming the resplendent melody of Mydei’s quickened heart.

“Haikas,” he chided softly. An affectionate nickname. The best one he ever had the honour of hearing. “Love yourself first.”

He laughed wetly but didn’t feel the urge to cry. “So do you love yourself more than me?”

His eyes watered and the world blurred but it cleared again in a few blinks. It was more than happiness. He felt content. More so than ever before—settled and grounded. Like the winds of fate could grab hold of him to tear him apart and scatter the remains, but it would fail to even lift him from the earth.

Mydei huffed a laugh. “Focus on yourself before your opponent.” 

His fingers dragged through his overgrown bangs, pinning them to the side so there was nothing between their eyes. The warmest sunrise, overflowing with affection just for him. Knowing everything about him and everything he had ever done. Loving him, not in spite of those things, but simply as another part of him that belonged right here in Mydei’s arms.

Mydei leaned up, breath hot against Phainon’s lips when he whispered, “But, if you find you’re unable to, know that I will love you in your stead until you can.”

Phainon kissed him. It was somehow exactly as he remembered—the feel of Mydei’s lips, the angle they tipped their heads, the length of time they could indulge in one another until the ache in his chest wasn’t his heart but his lungs—yet just different enough he knew it wasn’t a mere dream or memory yearning for the past. It was something new built from all the old things they had once been.

When Mydei pulled away, a hand on Phainon’s chest to keep him back so they could both catch their breaths, Phainon didn’t push. Not even a little.

He only grinned as he panted. “We should go out for breakfast tomorrow.”

Mydei’s chest heaved under him but he hummed. “Honeycakes?”

“Whatever you want. My treat!” And he sealed that promise with a quick peck to Mydei’s lips. “I have a lot of meals to pay you back for.”

“That depends,” Mydei drawled, voice still breathy as tipped his head into a smirk, “how many times have we been wed by now?”

Wed…

Phainon’s jaw slackened, gaping dumbly as his mind stuttered.

Mydei pinched his chin and left another kiss, one on his upper lip and a second on his bottom lip, accompanied by a nibble despite lidded eyes holding Phainon’s unseeing gaze the entire time. “Isn’t it natural for me to take care of my husband?”

“You…” Phainon swallowed, mouth dry, and Mydei’s grin grew. More lethal, more satisfied. “How underhanded.”

“And what am I trying to win exactly, husband?”

His face burned. No, his entire body. But it wasn’t a scorching blaze that burned even bones. It was the gentle lick of a harmless flame toying with him. “I’m uncertain. But there’s no need for you to play games. You already have me at your side. For as long as you’ll allow it and long after. Even the cosmos can’t take me from your side.”

There was no altar or witnesses but he said it as a promise, a vow. And he watched Mydei’s eyes widen with understanding then soften as Phainon cupped their hands and kissed the back of his ring finger.

After enduring suffering that corrupted hope and idealism, Phainon refused to run from the dawn he had chased for millions of cycles. Finally within his grasp—the life he had always wanted, with everyone. Amphoreus was where he truly belonged, alongside everyone who loved him as much as he loved them.

He would reunite with them all tomorrow in the light of a new dawn. One to be lived with all the care they were once robbed of and finally had the opportunity to flourish with love.

chapters.title: Afterword
chapters.html:
End Notes

One day I will write a fic from Phainon’s pov that doesn’t require him to suffer. That day was not any of the past few days I spent working on this.

His self-loathing and (perceived) inability to be loved is simply too delicious. I want to grab him and shake him violently while yelling about how much he deserves to be loved.

Extra from someone who hasn’t played 3.5:

[Chyrsos Heir meeting in the Hero’s Bath]

Anaxa: do we really still need to have these meetings here of all places?

Hysilens: I don’t see an issue

Castorice: I believe, Professor Anaxa—

Anaxa: Anaxagoras

Castorice: the baths are still the most convenient place for everyone to gather

Aglaea: but if your distaste for cleanliness is so great, none will stop you from making your exit. After all, we’re only here to discuss that dear child’s wellbeing

Anaxa: and pray tell, what is this ingenious plan of yours?

Aglaea: oh? You won’t even attempt to use that brilliant mind of yours

Anaxa: I’ve long given up trying to comprehend your actions, Aglaea

Mydei, clearing his throat: Phainon is in a very delicate state at the moment. We shouldn’t push him

Tribbie: poor snowy. He loves people so much and he’s locked himself and won’t see anyone

Cyrene: he really gets into his own head. After all this time, it’s worse than before.

Cipher: so we just need to break him out of it. I’m sure I can drag him out in a jiffy

Aglaea: that would be considered pushing him

Anaxa: We don’t know how stable he is physically and mentally. For all we know, he could blow up all of Amphoreus if he feels threatened

Cerydra: so our most effective weapon is undoubtedly…

Everyone: [looks at Mydei]

*a few weeks later*

Hyacine: Lord Mydei—

Mydei: considering the number of years we’ve confronted life and death together in the front-and back-lines, the formalities are unnecessary

Hyacine: Mydei, I noticed the dust on your leg when you came in. Did something happen?

Mydei: …

Anaxa: none of us can hear your mumbling. The bathwater is simply too loud

Aglaea: or perhaps your ears are as troubled as your eyes. It would certainly explain a few things over the years

Mydei: I kicked Phainon’s door down

Everyone: …

Castorice: what happened to not pushing him?

Mydei: that was foolish of me. That man responds best when pushed

Everyone: …

Aglaea: I see. Well, I’ve been preparing my own “push” so to speak

Mydei: perfect
